utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about the meetings that you had with state and military structures. Tell us, was there a leader in charge presiding over those meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring to the meetings held in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I mean. You told us that in the evening you had meetings with representatives of state organs and representatives of the military, that you attended it, the head of the staff, the deputy General Obrad Stevanovic, and you yourself, and that these were co-ordination meetings. So shall I -- I'm asking you: Was there a leader who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no one who would be a leader. We were the police, the army, and the political representatives who were there, we were at the same level so that no one had a leading or a commanding role.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At these meetings did you assign any tasks to police and army units?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those meetings the next task would be specified in keeping with the global plan, and we discussed the planning documents that would be elaborated for that purpose. There were no specific orders issued to the effect that perhaps the next day commands would be issued to someone to discharge that task -- to that effect, no. We had a general plan on the basis of which documents, specific documents, were drawn up and those documents would then be realised in practice to give effect to the global anti-terrorist plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up document P688, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your serial number 85 in your binder, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, these are minutes from the staff meeting of the 28th of July, 1998. Did you attend this staff meeting, and have you seen these minutes?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at the minutes. Three days after the beginning of the first operation that we had down there in the Kosovo area, the minister arrived with the intention of holding a meeting with the staff and be satisfied for himself of the state security situation and the way the work was being done. As according to his orders, also my primary duty was for activities in the field. I asked him by telephone for me to be excused from the meeting, and he agreed. So this meeting was held in my absence, and I was in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that escorting him and attending the meeting was also the deputy -- the assistant minister General Rade Markovic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is obvious from the minutes that the meeting was attended by Rade Markovic and staff members, MUP members, as well as heads of the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did mention this yesterday, but in addition to you, yourself, and General Obrad Stevanovic, during the -- were other assistants there and stayed for a while in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija during the realisation of this global plan?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Radomir Markovic on this particular occasion I believe that orders of the minister, he was dispatched to the area of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, and he attended a joint meeting, that joint meeting which was held that evening, and he actively contributed to the discussion. In July the assistant minister, Jovica Stanisic, also arrived in Kosovo and he also attended our co-ordination meetings with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, you said assistant minister Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, the head of the -- chief of the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And of the military personnel, were there any military attending the co-ordination meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were military senior officers who when visiting the Pristina units or the Pristina Corps would come there, and we met with them. They also actively participated in these meetings. As far as I can recall, General Samardzic, the commander of the 3rd Army, was there and there were also some lower-ranking commanders, officers who occasionally attended these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you on the 28th of July? You just told us that you were somewhere in the field where some activities were unfolding.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day the security forces were undertaking the final operations in order to enter Malisevo, which up to that point had been the principal stronghold of the terrorist forces and where their headquarters or their staff was which commanded their overall forces. As the situation was very serious, or rather, the action was very serious, I asked the minister to allow me to be there in the field on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you enter Malisevo then when that action was over?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We, or rather, the units active on the planned axes, those of major resistance, prior to entering Malisevo itself and when the resistance was crushed and the barricades dismantled there no longer was any resistance to us to enter the place of Malisevo proper, and in view of the fact that there was no resistance the commanding officers of the police and the army who were there reduced the use of all their assets. And practically this action of entering Malisevo did not entail any damage, but rather total control of the village was gained because the terrorists had already left the village with all the civilians so that there was no reason and there was no need for employing any assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was in charge of this action?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This action was conducted by military and police forces operating from two directions, from two axes. There were two police units and one military unit on each, and everyone commanded their own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who commanded the police?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was commanded by the commanders of the PJPs, namely, on one axis Special Anti-Terrorist Unit was employed commanded by its commanding officer, and the PJPs were commanded by their regular commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your role?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated that it was practically the most important action because the fiercest resistance was expected then because actually at that time Malisevo was being promoted as their centre, their stronghold, the centre of that republic. So for those reasons, as there were many police and army units participating, a large number of people, of men in other words, and since the situation was unfamiliar, I wanted to participate. I practically was an observer there, so if the situation should actually deteriorated I wanted to be of assistance, to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So now we have come to Malisevo. Tell me, before that sometime in mid-July were there any terrorist activities from Orahovac to Malisevo, Zociste, Padaliste, and that area there?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an area where there were markedly pronounced terrorist activities. Practically from Malisevo through some forbidden [as interpreted] passes one reached Orahovac, and sometime in mid-July 1998 the terrorists had taken -- took a part of Orahovac. And all in all, this area, Malisevo, Orahovac, Suva Reka, Dulje, Blace, and again towards Malisevo, this -- these were territories under terrorist control and their activity there was indeed intensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D386, which is -- should be a video recording.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The white building is the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's watch for a little while more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the only civilian who remained there whom I saw on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, is this is what Malisevo looked like? Was this the state that it was in on the 28th of July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, that was the state the place was in when the police forces came to the entry point into that place. There was a petrol station at the entry point. I came and some assistants of the minister. I asked them to convey the message to the minister that we were there at the entry point into Malisevo, and the next day the spokesperson of the MUP - at that time it was Colonel Bozidar Filic - came together with journalists. They came, and they toured Malisevo. It's a small place. You could see the small shops and businesses. That is what we found when the police forces entered. Practically not a single building was damaged at the time when we took control of the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: While we still have this video --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at D010-1756.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while it is brought up, perhaps we could clarify whether the witness said at page 6, line 21 Colonel Bozidar Milic - if that is the correct name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell us again the name of the colonel.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozidar Filic, F, Filic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have -- Marie, maybe we could proceed with another document and then when you are ready with this one, we'll present it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to the comments on this video, tell me for the record, who was with you when you were entering Malisevo on the 28th of July? Who were you with?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were commanders of the police and army units. At that moment, there were no other personalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, tell us, did you see these fortifications that we could see on the video?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them only on video footage, not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This was just an illustration. Did fortifications actually on the ground look like this, or could you describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely like these, in some places even better and stronger. There were really trenches several kilometres long dug according to all army regulations, and I can say that in terms of engineering and fortification they did the job really professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We saw on the video a moment ago this vehicle, the armoured vehicle of the police damaged. Did the KLA have weapons capable of destroying such vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had both the weapons, and sometimes they improvised weapons, built them manually. This weapon was charged with explosive and other material, and they simply detonated the device, this improvised device, when our vehicle would be arriving, vehicles carrying personnel as well. And they also used traditional anti-tank mines by placing them on roads or by the road, but they also had anti-armour weapons such as hand-held launchers and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We've just seen a trench and very tall corn-stalks above them. You said at one point that the police was ambushed from such fields. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see at this point in the video footage this corn could not burn because the vegetation is rich, but in the month of August in the course of certain activities, there were fields with crops that had not been harvested yet. And during anti-terrorist actions and attempts to break their resistance, the exchange of fire between police and terrorists and the use of various weapons would sometimes set these fields on fire because the crops were very dry and the temperature was high. It burned very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were there any deliberate torchings of these fields?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no reason to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P133. Excuse me, can I ask the last video to be admitted into evidence first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D428.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Here we see a letter of the 28th of July, 1998. Would you tell us, who is it addressed to and tell us a little about the contents. How did this come about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a classical letter describing the sending of PJPs to execute special security tasks - in this case in Kosovo - and to replace units sent before. In this case the units specified here are sent, and the letter is addressed to all secretariats so that each secretariat can see what its particular obligations are. So the administration of the police was involved because special -- because members of the PJPs were being sent on special missions. It says where the units are being sent, where they are to report, how they should be equipped, how their per diems should be paid, which routes they should take, and that is the format of all dispatches that deal with the sending of units or officers to special missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does it specify what exactly they would be doing?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first sentence says: To lend assistance in carrying out special security tasks. That is the only thing that we can read here. There is not a single sentence about a specific security task or the way in which it would be executed. Hereby, the units are only being sent to specific locations in order to obey others there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On whose orders were such units in Kosovo and Metohija acting in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in those two years. PJPs and the special unit of the MUP of Serbia was engaged exclusively on the orders of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But who gave them their specific tasks once they arrived in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They received their specific tasks from the secretariat where they were sent -- sent as assistants, or if the staff was in charge of whatever tasks they were to execute, then they received them from the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked you specifically in 1998 and 1999, from whom did they received their tasks?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, exclusively from the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P1201.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 87. Mr. Djordjevic, could you comment on this dispatch of the 14th of August, 1998. This is in fact a Teletype text.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this dispatch was sent to all organisational units within the sector and some units outside of the sector, such as the police academy, the college of internal affairs, and the secondary school of internal affairs. It describes abuses of sick leave because certain members did not want to serve within special units and try to avoid it, and the other matter is training, accommodation, certain status-related matters that apply to all members of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P886 now and -- to begin with -- now this will be difficult. Page 12 in B/C/S and page 16 of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, don't look in the binder, it's not there, you can only see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's a big document, but we have to see Mr. Pavkovic, Djordjevic, Lukic -- is this page 16 in English? The Serbian is good. Let's see the bottom -- next page then. No, no. Can we see the next page in English. No. Can we try to see the date of this meeting in Serbian, just to see the date of the meeting. This page is good, K022-8423. 26th of July. In English -- in the English one it is the 28th of July. Can we look for the 26th of July in the English version. The B/C/S version is just right quite. Let's see page 8 then. July 26. Let us just go to the next page to locate this section which corresponds to the -- another page, please. That's it. We have Mr. Djordjevic here. And can we see page 12 of the Serbian version, please. Scroll down, scroll down, please. We want to see Djordjevic in the English version, please. It should be page 12, 12 in the Serbian and 12 in the English version. Okay. Can you zoom in on Mr. Djordjevic in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is that you were talking about here.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm unable to read it. I cannot see it all, but basically at these meetings we exchanged information on everything, everything that was going on in the field or activities which needed to be further regulated, adjusted in the plan in keeping with developments in the field. Along those lines I gave my views and my contributions at all these meetings, informing the present about what I had personally seen in the field, my intention being for us to discharge our duties successfully, to give effect to the general plan. I cannot see, I'm not able to read exactly what it was on that particular occasion, what it says here, The plan was -- I really -- I probably said something along the lines of that the tasks were overambitious and that we were to either reduce their scope or something to that effect as far as this specific day is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you this also: On the basis of your input at meetings like these, did comment of the Pristina Corps and the staff, did they take decisions and implement those decisions in realising specific plans?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the participants at the meeting would state their opinions, and whatever input was amenable to the realisation of the general plan would be accepted and other contributions would not be accepted. Practically at these meetings we exchanged all the information that we had available in order for us to be able to successfully discharge our assigned tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on to July 27, 1998. That is page -- it is K022-8424 in B/C/S, and it is page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please zoom in on the -- this section which is in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where it says, "Gen," G-e-n, "Djordjevic," directly under the number which is in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on that axis, on that road, and this was the second day of activities to liberate, so to speak, this road. There is reference to the village of Mlecane where there were barricades, and I talked about that at the meeting. I said that there were concrete barricades, I believe, and I informed the meeting of that fact. Also whilst working in the field there was an accident. A policeman from the special unit got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down the English text, please, to see another contribution of General Djordjevic's. Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you also spoke a bit later. Can you read out for us what it was that you said?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Along that road there were quite a few activities and fighting with the terrorists because we neutralised quite a few of their strongholds along that road, and I informed all present that there were no civilian -- that there had been no civilian casualties and that in the villages that I saw by the road there were no civilians at all, and that was also a bit of information which I offered to the assembled meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move on to page 14 of the B/C/S version. The date is the same. It is K022-8425. Fine. In my document it says page 19 in the English version -- no, rather, it's page 14 in the English. Can you scroll down page 225 in the Serbian version so that we can see where General Djordjevic is indicated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it should be scrolled down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no. Where it says it should be solved, General Djordjevic, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. The written version should go down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you -- look at the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I see it at the bottom of the page. The village of Dusevic must be resolved, and the villagers should enter the village. Well, this was a general practice, namely. In all our activities we established that there were no villagers there and that later they would be found as displaced persons in some other locations not far from the villages where they had taken shelter because of the activities which were being carried out by the terrorist forces targeting the police and vice versa and not infrequently also according to the instructions of the terrorist forces when it suited them. We decided to have all the villagers return to their villages and as far as -- and as far as possible to continue living normal lives because no action of the police was ever directed at civilians. However, there were all kinds of abuses by KLA members and there were many villages where all the villagers were in the village and the police forces passed by, going about their duties. There was no resistance put up to the police. There were no attacks on the police so that this unfolded normally, and the police went about their regular duties without any such resistance being offered, but unfortunately there were also villages from which such resistance was offered because they were the strongholds of terrorists who pursued their activities from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now get page K022-8436 in the B/C/S version. That ought to be page 34 in the English version. Page 26 of the B/C/S version, please. It should be page 26 in the English version as Marie just told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You can of course consult the left side -- the left-hand side in the Serbian, but if you can, you can also read the English. So ... please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the earlier principle, namely, according to what I had observed in the field or what I had been told in the field, I would inform and point to the security -- out the security situation in the vicinity of the village of Dulje and elevation 925 and the Klecka area. And I'm not quite sure what the last sentence reads, Near Ostrozub three men were captured and ten were killed -- I'm not sure what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is the 31st of July, 1998; right?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The activities on the 31st of July had to do with the lifting of the blockade of the -- on the Pristina-Prizren-via Dulje road, and the road having been cleared, they proceeded towards where the assessed locations were of the KLA headquarters. Tell me -- it says here, ten -- Three were captured and then ten who were killed. What -- in what way?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the information given to me in the field that three terrorists had been captured, and as for the rest, I'm not sure whether Djakovic heard it and -- or how he heard it and how it was recorded. But at any rate, I reported that three had been captured and ten had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But were they killed in the activities, in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on to the 4th of August, 1998. It is page 33 in the B/C/S version, it's K022-8443. It should be page 33 in the English version, rather 32. I'm sorry. Can we see the next page in the Serbian version, 443. And the English also.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You see your name there, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. It says here, Execution of Albanians, 20 of them, near Lapusnik. So apart from this main task to free these roads, in view of the fact that there had been many kidnappings in the past period and we had intelligence that kidnapped citizens were kept in various basements, such as Orahovac, Albanians, Serbs, and others. So that was the context. When this road was again free, we had information that there was some sort of camp in Lapusnik. When our operation was completed an acquaintance called me from Urosevac and told me that he had an Albanian with him who had escaped an execution. Rizah Rexhaj was the name, and the name of the village he was from was Petrovo. And I went there, and I heard his story. He described how he had been in a camp not far from the main road in Lapusnik, he had been there with his father. He described how they were treated and mistreated. And when the police and army forces were lifting the blockade off that road, the people who kept them in the camp took them out and put them before a firing squad, but he ran to the woods not far from that site. Of course he was afraid and concerned about his father. He didn't know what had happened to him. To me it was a very interesting situation. I told him to report it to the SUP, and I called the chief of the SUP and asked him to take the necessary steps, to go to that area together with the man Rizah and to see if there were any bodies there. And the chief of the SUP sent a platoon of soldiers with the necessary equipment. They found the site of the camp. The man -- the man found some clothes belonging to his father, but they were unable to find any bodies of the people who had been, as he said, executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The person who kept this record wrote something here. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Execution of 20 Albanians - they were later taken to another place" --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the place is controlled by the KLA. That they were transferred to another territory deeper controlled by the KLA, and it says that I said: "Investigate the place above Lapusnik and see what's there." That's indeed what I said, to deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You explained that, Mr. Djordjevic. Just explain this execution of Albanians and 20 in brackets.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were Albanians, Serbs, and people of other ethnicities who were in this camp in Lapusnik. That's what I had been told by the man who had escaped from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who executed them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: KLA forces who controlled the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now get page 29, 2nd August 1998, K022-8440. Page 29 in English. This is good. Let us see the bottom of the page in B/C/S, thank you, where Mr. Djordjevic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So on the 2nd of August, 1998, what was the discussion about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about the implementation of the plan and the entry into one of the greatest strongholds of the terrorists in Jablanica village. We had to cross a lot of territory to get there and many other villages. Here I inform all those present that the units approaching Jablanica - and I was there too - Jablanica village being populated by ethnic Albanians who were Catholics, all the villagers had found refuge in the local church. And the terrorists had set ablaze some haystacks around the village but dispersed when they saw the police approaching. Therefore, there was no serious fighting and the village was not damaged, and all the villagers were hiding in the church, over 200 of them. When we got there we met with the people, talked to them, and as we were leaving people were going back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to the 19th of August, 1998. That's page 52 in B/C/S, K022-8462. And in English it's 52. It's at the top of the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Djordjevic, what did you say here?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As before, I reported on these activities and where they were carried out, in keeping with the plan; described the consequences; I shared what I knew at that moment as far as the police force is concerned; I told those present that the resistance in that area from Orahovac to Suva Reka was very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I see you also mention that some rifles were surrendered and some weapons were found?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some peculiar cases. Here I mention one hand-held launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And towards the end?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Rogovo has handed over 30 to 40 rifles and so has Kapesnica village," Kapesnica being another village where there were a lot of terrorists with a lot of weaponry, and Rogovo had received weapons from the terrorists and then they turned over, surrendered, 30-40 rifles of their own free will. That's what I reported at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to the 20th August 1998, page 55 B/C/S, K022-8466. English page 54. If we could see the lower part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, do you see at the bottom of the page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in SUP Pec I received this information that Rogovo village has surrendered three sub-machine-guns, 19 semiautomatic rifles, six hand-held launchers, et cetera. I reported what I learned during my stay there, and I -- what I thought was important for all those present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but in bullet point 5 you're mentioning a person from Lipovica.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see, this comes from a report we received when a person came in and said that there were 30 [as interpreted] to 400 persons kidnapped, both Serbs and Siptars being held there, but that is just me sharing something that I heard. I don't think the number is realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said the number was not realistic. What is written in this record?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says there were 300 to 400 kidnapped persons, and that's a lot for one location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to 4 September 1998. It's 75 in B/C/S, K022-8486, and page 73 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see this? Your contribution is in the middle of the page. Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see the way it's written here. I'm not sure I used those words, but never mind. As in prior occasions we were really very concerned about the civilian population, and we were anxious that after all these operations that had been carried out for villagers to return to their homes as soon as possible. Now, there were various problems. We were wondering on whose orders they had left, on whose orders they were staying away from their homes, and I suggested -- it says here that I suggested to bring them back by force, but I don't think that's what I was trying to say. I was trying to say that villagers should return to their villages as soon as possible and continue to live there and that we should persuade them in direct contacts that there was no reason to stay away. And this was not only one situation but in all other similar cases wherever we found civilians hiding somewhere away from their village in groups of one, two, three, or a thousand. We always wanted them to go back to their homes as soon as possible and continue to live normally, and we would always try to get them to return home whenever we found groups of several thousand people hiding somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the -- you were talking about the objectives of the police and forces and the authorities. How about the objectives of the KLA and the reactions of various diplomatic missions and journalists?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just finish with this. The first point says that villagers should be returned to the villages by force, and the fourth point is important, Action against terrorists. These two points are distinct. On the one hand, civilians should be returned to their homes and we should continue to fight terrorists. Those who were found hiding away from their homes should be brought back, and then there were various interpretations given by all sorts of international organisations, humanitarian and others, who were all pointing out and highlighting the humanitarian problem. They were condemning the Serb forces, saying that it was allegedly their activities that caused a lot of harm and suffering to civilians, forcing them to leave their homes. There were situations in which this was true, but those civilians left their homes before the police arrived on orders they received from members of the KLA, this terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you just repeat what you said about the number of people you would find in villages and around villages. Could you repeat that part.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've just seen this picture from Malisevo. There was only one person. In Glodjane village, which was one of the main terrorist strongholds of Ramush Haradinaj, we found again one person alone. In other locations, in Pusto Selo there was only one man; in other places there were two or three. And in large columns of people on the move - and this would usually be in large places after the end of operations - large numbers of these civilians were in large groups in woods outside the village or perhaps a few kilometres outside a village where anti-terrorist actions took place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on to -- can we have the minutes of the 6th of September, 1999 [sic], that's page 82 in the B/C/S version. It is K022-8493 and page 72 in the English version. The 6th of September, 1998, is actually the date of the meeting. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see what is noted here as your words, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This fits into the general pattern of conduct towards civilians. Then, namely after having learned that the villagers of a village - specifically in this case of Sedlare - were outside their village, I proposed that we go there with a company and return them through their villages, to talk to them, explain the situation to them, guarantee their security, and have them returned to their village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And this is under item 2, you say one company?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one company because this was a territory where there were also terrorists. So the villagers were in the woods near the village, and in order to ensure the safety of the policemen, I proposed that we go and see these refugee groups or provisionally displaced persons, temporarily displaced persons, with a company and to tell them to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, she didn't hear the beginning of this sentence of Mr. Djurdjic's, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: While we have General Lukic's contribution at the meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have not had co-ordination of the Serb and the English pages. The minutes of the 6th of September we've not had in English what the witness is speaking about, and now we have the meeting of the 7th of September, 1998, on screen in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether something has been changed. I was looking at the Serbian version. It was good. Can we now again see the 6th of September in the English version, please? The Serbian is good, just the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, this seems to be in English, minutes of the 6th of September, and at the moment we cannot see anything that compares to the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in the English version, please. Your Honours, at the bottom of the English version it is stated "General Djordjevic." Let us please not get confused. So far we have been dealing with September 6th, and these are the two versions that the accused talked about. Now we are moving on to the 7th of September. Do they correspond now, the two versions, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise and thank to you. Let us now move on to September the 7th, that is page 83 of the B/C/S version. It's K022-8494. We have the words of General Lukic. Let us not go through all of that. What I'm interested in is the fourth bullet point from the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see it, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Lukic is informing here that in keeping with what had been said the day before, a company was to try and to return the villagers to the village of Sedlare, and he is informing the meeting that they tried to do so but the KLA did not allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Read it out.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "An attempt was made to return to Sedlare with one company, but the KLA did not allow it." So this company actually met with the villagers who were outside the village of Sedlare and proposed to them that they return home, but they told the policemen that they could not because they were not allowed to do so by the KLA, the KLA forbade them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are still in the same document but page 84 of the Serbian version. It is K022-8495 and 82 of the English version. In the Serbian version it is right below these numbers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you comment on this. Here in the English version it's near the top after Mr. Minic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I commented on the use of artillery, and I suggested and pointed to the need to perhaps reduce the use of artillery, namely, that the artillery should not be used unnecessarily but only according to the concept which was that artillery should only be used to destroy their strongholds and that that would be the end of the use of artillery. And further action should be taken by police forces according to the plan which I earlier described. So I just pointed to the obligation of using artillery in keeping with the situation, namely, not unnecessarily, when it was not required for that particular field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the next?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke later, I pointed out the practices that I had encountered in the field and also learned of by talking to the heads of secretariats there, namely, that after police actions in fighting with the terrorists there would be subsequent torchings of -- or destruction of houses or of buildings where terrorist activities had already ended and that that territory should be protected by the territorial organs, by the SUPs, that they should prevent any such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were any measures taken to detect the perpetrators of these offences?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was a task issued by the staff to all, to the participants in the anti-terrorist activities, as well to the secretariats in the field. They were to take account of these matters and to take the legally envisaged measures against the perpetrators of these acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, in the implementation of this global plan, was any report being submitted to the relevant organs in Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, reports were being submitted. Generally speaking, as soon as a stage was completed we would convene a meeting, and we would update everyone on the progress made so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when did this reporting take place about the implementation, who attended, and who was specifically the person submitting this progress report?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the first meeting was held with the president of the FRY at the Beli Dvor, and the attendees were the same persons who had been present at the time when the plan was adopted. I think that the first such meeting took place after the implementation of this basic stage which involved the liberation of certain territories. It may have been in early August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who was there representing the Government of Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The President of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic; the Chief of General Staff and his associates representing the army; the minister of the interior; and the heads of both services, Obrad Stevanovic, the assistant minister, and the head of the Pristina MUP, General Sreten Lukic, basically all the people who were there at the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who submitted this progress report up to that stage?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion concerning the portion that the Army of Yugoslavia was engaged in was submitted by General Pavkovic, the commander of the Pristina Corps, providing all the details of how this was accomplished. On behalf of the Ministry of the Interior, the report was submitted by the head of the staff of MUP in Pristina, General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until this final implementation of the plan, did you have any other meeting with the highest leaderships of Yugoslavia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of August I think another meeting with the same composition and with the same agenda was held. The procedure was identical. All the people who reported before submitted reports this time again, and following the endorsement of these reports by the leaderships, also and indication was made of what was required to do in the forthcoming period and also we needed approval to continue with the implementation of this general plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have on our screens document 1145 from the Defence list, or rather, 4137 from the Prosecution's 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And in your binder, Mr. Djordjevic, it's number 58. Just a moment, please. Mr. Djordjevic, who has sent this dispatch and when?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a dispatch sent on the 14th of September to the office of the minister of the interior by the head of the staff, General -- Major-General Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of information does this dispatch relate to?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch relates to a previous dispatch sent on one day before, where basically and probably the information about the same event was provided, but here we have some additional details that the head of the staff wanted to inform the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you familiar with the situation in Istinic, and what do you know about the content of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is practically confirmation of what I said before, which is to say that members of the police wanted the civilians to go back to their homes and that at the level of the secretariat talks were being held with displaced persons; however, in certain international organisations, having their own agendas in a way, wanted to prevent the fulfilment of these obligations in an appropriate manner. In this letter Major-General Lukic points out some activities carried out by the representatives of the International Red Cross, who practically did not want the civilians to accept the offer from the police and return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have any direct experience, or were you in the village of Istinic at the time? If so, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is mid-July, if I'm not wrong -- or rather, this is the 10th of September, actually, so mid-September. At that time we had certain intelligence that in that area there were civilians, and we were discussing how to return them to their homes because there were people from some other villages as well. I personally wasn't present there, but I was there towards the end of September when a large-scale operation was being carried out in the area from Jablanica and Glodjane which were known to be strongholds of the terrorists. And since the terrorists had re-captured these areas, we launched a new action against them. At that moment we were faced with a large crowd of civilians in this village, so I'm talking about the end of September. At that time I was in the area of the secretariats of Pec and Djakovica, or rather, the municipal secretariat of Decani. I'm talking about the time when one of these final operations was in progress. I was there with the head of the section of the interior, Mircic, who informed me that he had intelligence about tens of thousands of civilians who were in Istinic and who had come from some 20-odd villages in the area. These villagers found shelter there because of the operation that was ongoing and probably as instructed by the terrorist organisations. He told me that if all these actions were to be carried through as planned and since the village of Istinic was sealed off, one would expect that the terrorists would put up fierce resistance in the area. And his estimate was - given that he was quite familiar with the situation there - that in the clashes and neutralisations of their strongholds, the result -- they might result in a large number of civilian casualties. In these talks he proposed that because he had good relations with ethnic Albanians to send someone to the village and to demand or to convey a message for the terrorists to move away from the barricades, to surrender their arms, and also that the civilians who had been given the weapons by the terrorists should do the same. In other words, they should not put up any resistance to the police in order to avoid huge civilian casualties in this fighting with the terrorists. I accepted this proposal of his, believe that this could contribute to solving the situation in a peaceful way and without any consequences for the civilians. He did send this person to the Istinic village, and he gave them a certain time-limit. I think this man went at around 11.00 and the time-limit was 1600 hours in the afternoon, by which they were supposed to leave the barricades and the police would then come in and collect the weapons, both from the terrorists and from the civilians who had received them from the terrorists. About an hour or two later this person came back and informed the chief of the OUP that his instruction has been accepted and that at 1600 hours all the barricades would be removed and that no armed persons would be positioned there because all the weapons will be collected by that time. The only thing left to do was for us to wait until 1600 hours to see how the situation was going to develop. In the meantime, the president of the Decani municipality arrived and the chief of the OUP, and he discussed this issue. We had information that there was a really huge crowd of people, so the issue was raised of providing assistance to these people if the outcome was to be the one as we expected. The president of the municipality called the president of the provisional Executive Council of Kosovo, Mr. Zoran Andjelkovic, and informed him about a potentially high number of civilians in the areas and told him that these civilians should be given help and assistance given their numbers and the situation that they were in. After receiving his call, Zoran Andjelkovic came to the area of the municipality, and we all met there at the president of the municipality's office. He undertook certain measures to ensure some basic first aid in food and other necessities for the citizens. At 1600 hours, as previously agreed, we entered, or rather, passed by these barricades that had been abandoned, meaning Zoran Andjelkovic, the president of the municipality, the chief of the OUP, myself, and some other people. We entered the village and from the opposite direction we saw some [indiscernible] people from the village, they had a tractor full of weapons. We greeted each other, and indeed there were quite a few civilians in the village. In addition to the weapons that had been left there, we also parked a truck in the centre of the village where the villagers brought their weapons on their own initiative and left it with the police. Zoran Andjelkovic asked all presidents of local communes from these villages to come to a meeting. We had reached an agreement with all these senior people or village elders, Albanians, because our primary desire was to organise gradually their return to their respective villages. In the meantime, all the police or military activities ceased. The situation was resolved in a peaceful way. We also discussed on that occasion how to make sure that everyone goes back to their village. After that, the president of the provisional Executive Council brought a few trucks full of milk and bread, some shops were opened, and this food was distributed to the people who were there. This process of returning people to their villages lasted, based on the agreement with all the prominent people from their villages, about two or three days. I was there on the first day when we reached this solution, as I described, without the use of force, without any damage or any consequences whatsoever. The officers from the regional secretariat remained there in order to ensure that everyone got back. They provided buses in co-operation with the local socio-political communities. Anyway, two or three days later practically all the villagers returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, please repeat the part when you entered the village, the group of people that you were with, how many civilians were there in the village then?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village was, so to speak, occupied by civilians. There was a huge crowd like at a football match.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was just for the record.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several thousand civilians were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I ask for this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D429.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, did you have any other similar experience with civilians in some other place?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in many places, starting with several civilians up to several thousand civilians. There was this remote village, this deserted village, beneath the slopes of Mount Koznik [as interpreted] when the civilians due to the imminent terrorist activities had taken shelter at the foot of that mountain and also villagers from the nearby villages had done so. There was a shoot-out on the next day with members of the terrorist group. Normally they withdrew in the direction of those civilians. In the village we found only one civilian, and not far from that village some 4 to 5 kilometres away at the foot of the mountain were all the villagers from that village as well as from other villages at the foot of the mountain as well as in the general area, in the wooded sections of the area. The civilians who were found on that occasion were escorted by the police to the centre of the village, and all other civilians who were on other locations were informed by the police that they should arrive at the centre of the village for consultations, for an agreement to be reached. And the political echelons were also informed that these civilians had been found so that the municipality provided urgent aid in food and other supplies. Medical aid was also provided. And in agreement with the police commanders on the spot, all the village elders assembled, were met with, and agreement was reached for them for the villagers to return to their homes, and many did so within a couple of hours. Others who so wished were rendered assistance by the police which escorted them to their homes in their villages in order to prevent them from coming to any harm or being attacked. At any rate, they all went to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, what village beneath -- beneath -- at the foot of this mountain was in question?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Pusto Selo, if I'm not mistaken. And there was similar situations elsewhere. On this particular occasion all the people who were taken in this refugee group that had taken shelter there were returned to their homes. There were perhaps some ten-odd citizens that we had grounds to believe at that time that they were perhaps members of the KLA who had discarded their weapons. So these ten or so people were on the basis of that suspicion apprehended, taken to the police station there. And in their processing in conjunction with the state security people, we established whether they did or did not belong to the KLA, and if it had been proven that they have been -- were members of the KLA and had participated in the fighting, then criminal proceedings were instituted against them followed by a normal traditional procedure and those who were established not to have been all of that were let go and released to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can we now have P1202. It's 89 your tab, Mr. Djordjevic. Your Honours, I have the impression that the transcript has stopped at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Djurdjic, I don't think it's your fault. It's being attended to. I think you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, please take a look at this dispatch. I believe it is of the 18th of September, 1998. Who are the addressees, and what is the subject?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior pursued a permanent operational action, the name of which was Sat, and it envisaged measures and activities by the secretariat aimed at preventing terrorist activities in the area of Serbia generally. This is a dispatch dated the 18th of September, 1998, namely from a time when anti-terrorist activities had already been undertaken in Kosovo, and at that point it was assessed in the ministry that there existed the possibility of terrorist activities from Kosovo spilling over to the rest of the territory of the Republic of Serbia and that by way of clockwork or other mechanisms the damage could be inflicted on significant facilities in Serbia. This dispatch is in that connection and in conjunction with the previous dispatch it instructed that additional attention should be devoted and additional measures taken in order to prevent a spillover of terrorist activities from Kosovo to the rest of Serbia. That is the substance of this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who signed this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- all the documents related to this basic action that were in existence for several years in the ministry, the entire file was in the police administration and all instructions and orders were actually issued by the police administration to be executed in the field. Therefore, this was signed by authority given him by me -- actually, I can only suppose judging by the handwriting by Ljubomir Aleksic, who was the deputy head of the police. And he signed this because this dispatch was to be forwarded to all the SUPs, to the ministry's staff, to the border police posts, and to other public security department organisational units. And as he as a deputy head of the administration could not convey a dispatch of this type to these organisational unit in his own name, that is why it was signed in my name. But again, this job and this task was discussed - and I'm quite sure of that - at the collegium meeting called by the minister. And it was at that collegium meeting that the minister actually gave orders that measures should be taken to pursue this action. And this dispatch only pointed out the additional measures to be taken in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic, we had stoppage in the record, in the LiveNote, while you were replying to my previous question. When you said that there were several tens or ten or so persons who were suspected of being KLA members, that they had been brought into the responsible SUP. So please complete that answer for the sake of the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think you need to. It will be picked up, I believe, in due course. It will be on the tape. No need to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We shall now move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you tender the dispatch of the 18th of September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It is already a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is already an exhibit in the file. Can we now see D244.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, now I shall like us to broach a subtopic related to this topic, and I shall use this dispatch by the MUP staff dated the 20th of September, 1998, concerning the handing over of weapons for that purpose. Can you tell me what information you had about that, what was the situation like in KiM territory in September and at the end of September in 1998 in this regard?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information about large quantities of weaponry having been brought in especially from Albania to Kosovo, both light infantry arms as well as heavier weaponry up to recoilless guns. In view of such intelligence as well as in view of our -- the information that we had that such weapons had been in fact distributed by force to certain people or to certain villages, measures were taken primarily to have this -- these weapons obtained from terrorists and which -- the source of which was illegal entry into Kosovo had to have them handed over to the Ministry of the Interior, i.e., the secretariats in Kosovo. It was to that end that head of the staff issued these instructions to the heads of the secretariats, pointing out the issue and the way in which to register the received weapons and in which way to report back to the MUP staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see document 0068-0558.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is 92 in your tab, and it is 918 according to the Defence 65 ter list. Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D008-0558. Can we please see page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Acting according to the instructions in the dispatch that we just saw, this is an example of how the SUP in Djakovica received weapons from citizens in their area. The authorised officials of that secretariat drew up a record of the hand-over of weapons, ammunition, and mines and explosives, and then on the pages that follow they indicate the type of weapons, their numbers. And on the last page there is a recapitulation of the weaponry returned up to that point in time in the area of just that secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4, here we see what one could call hand-held weapons, but on page 4 we also see some other types of weaponry. Can you tell us what these are?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are listed according to type, beginning with light infantry, then through sub-machine-guns, and then machine-guns which are very heavy but still an infantry weapon, and then hand throwers, hand launchers, several types of them, rocket-launchers, hand-held rocket-launchers, several pieces, mines, grenades, explosives, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D430.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see document D008-0569. It is 919 for the Prosecutors according to the 65 Defence list, 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And for you, Mr. Djordjevic, it is tab 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a record on the hand-over of weapons in the organisation of the unit Decani. That's an organisational unit of the secretariat in Djakovica. And according to the same principle, all types of weapons are listed, they are usually made in China. I think, and the date seems to correspond, that these were weapons turned over by civilians when we entered the village of Istinic in the way that was agreed. We must emphasise here that on that occasion, it says on page 8, 70 sub-machine-guns of one type were handed over -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are three pages in the English document, I'm afraid, Mr. Djurdjic, so there's no page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were saying about sub-machine-guns, Mr. Djordjevic. What else was turned over?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sub-machine-gun is a very dangerous weapon and almost 200 of them were handed over this time but also 50 hand-held launchers made in China and very typical six recoilless guns. These are the heaviest calibres, an artillery weapon that the terrorist forces had, so early in the territory of Decani six recoilless guns were turned over and one mortar 82-millimetres and 760-millimetre [as interpreted] mortars. These are very serious weapons that the terrorists had that were turned over by the -- to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received, Mr. Djurdjic, but there is a difficulty -- the Serbian has 12 or so pages, the English 3. There's a mystery there somehow which needs to be looked at and resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me explain. The translations, quite smartly, did not list all the serial numbers of these automatic rifles. We have page 3 here where it says, Chinese hand-held launches from one to 53. They did the same with rifles, and instead of listing all the serial numbers that the police needs, they did not include that in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be, I believe, Exhibit D431.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, for the record, while we're still at this document we have this 60-millimetre mortars. How many of them, how many 60-millimetre mortars, are mentioned in the document?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven mortars of 60-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This was admitted. Now I'd like you to go back to D245. It's your tab 91. Mr. Djordjevic, this is a staff document of 2nd of October, 1998. Were you aware of this? Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know about this. The highest authorities in Serbia were informed of the number, the quantity of weapons turned over up to that point, and also the amount of weapons still at the disposal of ethnic Albanians that they were forced to accept from the terrorists. Now, proceeding from these assessments of how serious the situation was, the Assembly of Serbia at its session of 28th September decided to invite ethnic Albanians who had been forced to accept weapons to turn over those weapons to the competent authorities, promising them that no steps would be taken against them, although possession of such weapons constituted a crime. So the Assembly of Serbia is practically offering amnesty to all such citizens so that they may return such weapons without suffering any consequences. And in keeping with that conclusion of the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, the staff issues tasks to secretariats, telling them what to do in order to collect weapons in this drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D009-0769. That would be 65 ter 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And your tab 94. Unfortunately we still have not received the translation. Translation is pending. Can you tell us what kind of information this is. We see it comes from the ministry staff. It concerns operations carried out to fight terrorism in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. Mr. Djordjevic, first tell us, to whom was this addressed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was made for the minister and the staff provided information that it had specifically concerning the period from the 1st to 25 July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That is the first i. What about ii?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, terrorist attacks and outcome; and number ii, combat activities. It's a very brief report covering only the units engaged in these combat activities, how many anti-terrorist actions had been carried out, and the main results described in a few sentences, lifting the blockade of roads or sections of the roads, which routes, et cetera. All this information you can find in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, could you read -- could you read from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you read, I just wonder if we could be told whether it's dated and if it's signed by who and how he knows about it. How he's able to speak to its contents. I know it refers to the period 1st to 25th of September, but we don't know the date. We don't know if it's signed by somebody, if a particular person sent it, what basis it is that he speaks about it. In documents that are translated, these things are obvious on the face of it, but here I'm just in a vacuum, listening in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unfortunately we don't have the translation. We could see that from the first page. This document was received from the National Council at the Ministry of the Interior for the area of Kosovo and Metohija. Unfortunately, we don't have the date here, but on the first page of this document provided by the MUP it says: "Information of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija about operations to fight terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, anti-terrorist actions, combat activities, impact on civilians, ways of securing the liberated territory" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel read a little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the chapters of -- various chapters are described here. On the first page of the document it says, Information on operations executed to fight terrorism in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. There is no signature. It's just the report, a brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting it was prepared by the National Council or merely that it was stored by the National Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. While reviewing the documentation at the Ministry of the Interior, I saw this document and then I requested through the national counsel for the document to be made available to me to use in this court, and the National Council made it available to me. And I then showed it to the accused in proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, we haven't yet heard whether the witness knows anything about this document and its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You've heard the question, Mr. Djordjevic. I don't want to -- I don't need to reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all about the contents of this document because I was directly involved for a good part. All the activities of the staff are familiar to me, especially from the period when I was there myself. And from this material, I don't see exactly but I assume it was done for the minister and for his purposes, so that he can use it to brief others. But it covers the information available to the staff at that time. I was familiar with most of this information, the weapons, the movements of civilians, most of the combat activities, the activities to deblock roads, and I believe this material faithfully represents the situation prevailing at the time and the events unfolding. Most of these terrorist attacks and their consequences were reported to the ministry in daily reports, and it's also based on that information that the staff prepared this summary report chapter by chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, do we see in this material anything about the activities of both the public security and the state security departments?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we see the number of criminal reports filed by the state security and the number of persons named in these criminal reports, and also in the process of deblocking roads and in anti-terrorist activities the unit for special operations and the state security department JSO was involved, so their activities are also covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you turn to page 2 and read slowly the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, with -- I don't want to sound pedantic, but what the witness is saying is that he's aware -- or he thinks, he believes I think he said that the contents of the document are accurate, but he has not really testified about the document itself, the provenance of the document. It is neither signed nor stamped or dated. You know, he could be asked to read from a document that could have been created any time, anywhere, in any country. All he can say is that this looks true to me, but there are quite a lot of possibilities about the creation of documents that might contain contents that are true to him. The witness needs to speak, it is my submission, more about the document itself. Does he know about this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer is he has told us he does not. You're sounding almost like Mr. Djurdjic in some of the objections he made to your case, Mr. Stamp.
